## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="b1-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Formulate it</dt><dd>Every story becomes decisions (letters), a goal (a sum to minimize or maximize) and rules (inequalities).</dd>
<dt>Feasible region</dt><dd>The plans that keep every rule; with two decisions it is a shape on a plane.</dd>
<dt>Best corner</dt><dd>When a linear program has a best plan, one sits at a corner of the region.</dd>
<dt>Signs matter</dt><dd>≤ where the story says ≥ lets the model skip its job, and the answer still looks optimal.</dd>
<dt>A x ≤ b</dt><dd>Solvers read the costs c, a rule table A and limits b, with every rule written as ≤: x + y ≥ 145 enters as −x − y ≤ −145.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Why the best plan sits at a corner</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

All plans with the same cost $C$ lie on one straight line, $40x + 100y = C$: the dashed line of step 5. Lowering $C$ slides the line towards the origin without turning it. The cheapest allowed plan is the last point of the region the line touches as it slides, and a straight line leaving a region bounded by straight edges leaves it at a corner, here $(130, 15)$ at \$6,700.

Two footnotes. If the cost line is parallel to an edge, it leaves along the whole edge: both corners, and every plan between them, are equally good (try costs of \$40 and \$40). And if the region is open in the direction the goal pulls, there is no best plan: the solver reports the model as unbounded.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The same model in a modelling language</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Modelling languages let you write rules as algebra instead of arrays; they build $A$, $b$ and $c$ for the solver. The dispatch model in [JuMP](https://jump.dev/) (Julia), with [HiGHS](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/) as the solver:

```julia
using JuMP, HiGHS
m = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
@variable(m, 0 <= x <= 150)          # combined-cycle, MW
@variable(m, 0 <= y <= 100)          # peaker, MW
@constraint(m, cover, x + y >= 145)
@constraint(m, ramp, x <= 90 + 40)
@objective(m, Min, 40x + 100y)       # $ for the hour
optimize!(m)
value(x), value(y)                   # (130.0, 15.0)
```

In Python, [Pyomo](https://www.pyomo.org/) and linopy (the layer under [PyPSA](https://docs.pypsa.org/)) play the same role. Bridge B3 reads formulations written this way for many hours and plants at once, and the Modeler lesson M1 builds one for a whole day.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What these small models leave out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>One hour at a time: a real dispatch plans all 24 hours together, so the ramp links each hour to the next (B3, M1).</li>
<li>Plants are always available and can run at any level; real units have minimum outputs and start-up costs, which need on-off decisions (M2, upcoming).</li>
<li>Prices and capacity factors are fixed numbers; real studies vary them (lesson 12 and the Modeler tier).</li>
<li>Two decisions fit on a graph; real models have thousands to millions, which is why solvers exist.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="b1-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="strict" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A solver handles x &lt; 130 just as well as x ≤ 130.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. With a strict &lt; there may be no best plan: 129.9, 129.99 and so on are each better than the last. Linear programs use ≤ and ≥ only.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="corner" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If a linear program has a best plan, one of its corners is a best plan.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact, for regions with corners, as here. When two corners tie, every plan on the edge between them is best as well.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="zero" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the solver says ‘optimal’, the model is right.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. With the cover rule flipped to ≤, “optimal” meant making nothing for $0. Optimal is about the model, not the story: B3 teaches the checks.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="b1">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="loss" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">The battery's losses rule is d ≤ 0.9c. As a row of A x ≤ b, with x = (c, d):</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">(−0.9, 1) and b = 0</li><li data-value="b">(0.9, 1) and b = 0</li><li data-value="c">(0, 1) and b = 0.9</li><li data-value="d">(1, −0.9) and b = 0</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>(−0.9, 1) with b = 0: move 0.9c to the left, −0.9c + d ≤ 0. A zero on the right is common when a rule links two decisions.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="kind" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">“The peaker is either off, or on at 50 to 100 MW.” Is this still a linear program?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Yes, write 50 ≤ y ≤ 100</li><li data-value="b">No: it needs an on-off decision</li><li data-value="c">Yes, write y ≥ 0</li><li data-value="d">No: it needs a curved cost</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>No. “Off or at least 50” leaves a gap between 0 and 50, which no set of straight-line rules can describe; an on-off (binary) decision can. That is a mixed-integer program (M2, upcoming).</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="b1-practice"></div>
```
:::
